بيت: It is said: بيت, بيوت, and أبيات.
And from it is said that the poetic house is called بيت by analogy because it is a collection of words, letters, and meanings, on the specific condition of the meter.
And this is what the speaker meant:
And a بيت on the back of the mat I built... with the brown of the torn khayashim it glitters.
He meant by al‑asmar the pen.
And the بيت: the man's children and those who stay with him.
What a certain person has as a بيت for the night, i.e. what he stays on at night of food and other things.
And he settled the matter when he arranged it at night.
God Almighty said: {إِذْ يُبَيِّتُونَ مَا لَا يَرْضَى مِنَ الْقَوْلِ} [النساء: 108], i.e., when they gather in their houses.
Except that this is specific to the night.
And the بيوات: the water that stays overnight.
And the بيوات: the matter that its owner stays on, being concerned about it.
And I make its poverty a tool... when I fear the بيوات of a matter of hardship (unclear).
And the بيات and the tabyit: to bring the enemy at night, as if you have taken him into his house.
It is narrated from [أَبِي] عُبَيْدَةَ that he said: a thing is بيوت when it is destined, and this is likened to the destiny of poetic بيوت.
And this is not far from the original root that we derived and measured upon.
حمد: It is said: I praised so‑and‑so, I praised him.
And a man named Mahmoud and Muhammad, when his praised qualities are many, they are not blameworthy.
The cripple said: He praised al‑Nu‘man ibn al‑Mundhir, and it is said that he favored him with this word over everyone else he praised that day:
To you, O Abū al‑‘Lan, his speech was ... to al‑Majid, the noble, the generous, al‑Muhammad.
And for this one we mentioned, our Prophet was named Muhammad, peace be upon him and his family.
The Arabs say: may your desire be to do so, i.e., your aim and your deed are praised from you, not blameworthy.
It is said: I praised so‑and‑so when I found him praised, just as one says I was stingy with him when I found him stingy, and I found him incapable.
And this is a rule that is applied to all other attributes.
And I stirred the place when I found it hot, its plant may have withered.
And he stirred the pure gold from the lightning.
If a questioner asks about their saying in the voice of the burning fire of praise; they were told: This is not from that chapter, because it is from the twisted and its root is a bone.
And it has been mentioned in its place.
خط: And from that line which the writer writes.
And from it the line which the potter writes.
God Almighty said: {or a trace of knowledge} [Al-Ahqaf: 4]; they said: it is the line.
It is narrated: “Indeed a prophet among the prophets used to write, so whoever wrote like his writing knew like his knowledge.”
And from the chapter the line of the earth is drawn by a person for himself, because there is an extended trace there.
And from it the line of the dove, and to it the straight arrows are attributed.
And from the chapter the line, and it is the condition; it is said ‘by a line of evil’, because it is a matter that has been drawn for it and upon it.
As for the lined earth, which has not been rained upon between two irrigated lands, it is not from the chapter, and the second ‘ṭā’ is added, because one who errs is as if the rain erred.
The proof of that is the saying of Ibn ‘Abbas: “God made a mistake of its kind”, i.e., when another rain falls it errs, so it does not affect it.
And as for their saying: “On the head of so‑and‑so there is a line”, the people said: it is only a line.
If that is so, it is as if it is a matter that is drawn and has effect, as we have mentioned.
سلم: Scholars say: God, glorified is His praise, is peace; his safety protects creatures from defect, loss, and death.
God, glorified is His majesty, says: {And Allah calls to the abode of peace} [Yunus: 25]; thus peace is God, glorified is His praise, and its abode is Paradise.
Also from this category is Islam, which is submission, because one submits from the father and from abstaining.
And peace: the state of being safe.
And a verb that appears in the verbal noun often related to fighting and combat.
And from the section of companions and submission: the salām called salaf, as if it were a wealth that is given and not withheld from giving.
It may be that the stone was called silām because it is the farthest
thing on earth from decay and disappearance; because of its hardness and solidity.
As for al‑salīm, which is al‑ladiḡ, its naming contains two statements: one that it was submitted because of what it has.
And the other statement is that they exchanged greetings of safety.
And they may name a thing with names of optimism and speculation.
And the ladder (sullam) is known, and it is also from safety; because the one who descends upon it is hoped to have safety.
And safety: a tree, its plural is salām.
And the one that deviated from the door of peace: the dalw which has one branch.
And the salam: a tree, one of its kind is salama.
And the salāmān: a tree.
And from the first category, the silm is reconciliation, and it can be feminine or masculine.
God the Exalted says: {And if they turn to peace, then turn to it} [Al‑Anfal: 61].
And salima: the stone, in which the poet says:
That is my friend and one who reproaches me... he throws behind me with the arrow and the salima.
And the Banu Salima: a group of Ansar not found among the Arabs except them.
And among the names, Salma: a woman.
And Salma: a mountain.
And Abu Sulma, father of Zuhayr, with a doubled sin, is not found among the Arabs except him.
عبد: The first meaning is ‘the servant’, i.e. a slave, and the group is ‘the slaves’; three servants are ‘the worshippers’.
The companion said: except that the masses gathered on the distinction between the servants of God and the enslaved slaves.
This is said of a servant who is a clear example of worship.
We have not heard them use a verb from it; if they had, it would be said ‘abada’, meaning he became a servant and acknowledged worship, but the verb is dead and not used.
He said: as for ‘abada’ meaning to worship, it is said only of one who worships God‑the Exalted.
From him is said ‘abada’ meaning he worships, and ‘ta‘abbada’ meaning he worships intensely.
‘Ta‘abbudan’ (noun) – worship.
Thus ‘al‑mut‘abbid’ is the one who is unique in worship.
And I enslaved so‑and‑so: I took him as a servant.
And as for ‘‘abd’ meaning to serve one’s master, one does not say ‘abada’, nor say he worships his master.
And ‘ta‘abbada’ so‑and‑so, if he makes him like a slave to him even if he is free.
He said:
‘Ta‘abbadani Nimr ibn Sa‘d and I saw … and Nimr ibn Sa‘d is obedient and eager for me.’
It is said: ‘‘abada’ so‑and‑so so‑and‑so’, i.e. he made him a servant.
It is said of the polytheists: ‘the slave‑girl of the tyrant and the idols’; for Muslims: ‘worshippers who worship God‑the Exalted’.
Some of them said: ‘‘abid’ and ‘‘abada’, like servants and servants.”
The feminine of ‘abd’ is ‘‘abda’, just as ‘mamluuk’ and ‘mamluuka’.”
The companion said: ‘al‑‘ibada’: the group of slaves who were born into slavery.”
And from the chapter: ‘the worshipped camel’, i.e. the camel saddled with two loads.”
This also indicates what we said, because that humbles him and lowers him.”
The poet said:
‘Until the whole tribe protected me … and I singled out the lone worshipped camel.’
‘Al‑‘abud’: the humbled one, also used to describe the camel.”
And from the chapter: ‘the worshipped road’, which is the humbled, subjugated one.”
The other root is ‘‘abada’, meaning strength and firmness; it is said ‘this is a garment for him, ‘‘abda’, if he is a strong, sturdy companion.’
And from it comes ‘‘Alqama ibn ‘Abda’, with a fatha on the ba.”
From this analogy ‘‘abd’ is like ‘the nose’ and ‘the heat’.
It is said: ‘He worships this matter.’
It was explained: “Say, if the Most Merciful had a son, then I am the first worshipper” (Al‑Zukhruf 81), i.e. the first to be angry about this and to reject his statement.”
It is reported from ‘Ali ‑ peace be upon him ‑ that he said: ‘I worshiped and then was silent’, i.e. I worshiped and then fell silent.”
He said:
‘The ignorant one worships the arrogant by their right … after judgment upon him when there is no worship.’
And another said:
‘I worship that a dog is driven away by the reins.’
It is an expression meaning ‘I am angry about that and I resent it.’
قول: It is said: He said, he says, a statement.
And the spoken thing: the tongue.
And a man of speech and a speaker: one who speaks a lot.
كتب: From that, the book and the writing.
It is said: I wrote the book, I write it as a writing.
And they say: I wrote the mule, when I joined its two ribs with a knot.
He said:
Do not trust a foreigner, you have made it ... upon your palm and write it with bands.
And the writing: the splinter, and it was called that because of its gathered fragments.
And the written: the splinter.
He of al‑Rumma said:
And the overflow of a cavity that exhausted its pits ... a clatter that lost it among the writings.
And from the chapter, the book is the obligation.
God Almighty said: {كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ} [البقرة: 183], and it is said for a ruling: the book.
The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "As for I will judge between you by the Book of God Almighty", meaning his ruling.
And God says: {يَتْلُو صُحُفًا مُطَهَّرَةً} [البينة: 2].
{فِيهَا كُتُبٌ قَيِّمَةٌ} [البينة: 3], i.e., sound judgments.
And it is said for destiny: the book.
Al‑Jaʿdī said:
O daughter of my uncle, the Book of God brought me out ... from you and shall I prevent God what they did.
And from the chapter, the writings of horses, it is said: they wrote.
He said:
With an alif they wrote or a miqnab.
Ibn al‑Aʿrābī said: the writer among the Arabs is the scholar, and he argued with God's saying: {أَمْ عِنْدَهُمُ الْغَيْبُ فَهُمْ يَكْتُبُونَ} [الطور: 41].
And the correspondence: the servant writes to his master on his own.
They said: and its origin is from the book, meaning the condition that is written between them.
لبن: It is said: labintu his milk, al‑binu his milk, when you give milk to it; and so‑and‑so is labin, meaning he has milk, just as one says tamir.
And you deceived me and claimed that you … labin in summer tamir.

Al‑mulbin: great abundance of milk. A she‑camel called labinah is very milky; when its milk falls on its udder it is mulbin, and if it has milk it is labun, a great or thin abundance. A man mulboun is foolish for drinking too much milk. The milk‑fattened horse, the one fed with milk, is preferred. It is said: how much wool of your sheep and its milk, i.e., how many milk‑possessing females it has.

From what deviates from this entry [milk]: neck pain from a pillow, a man is called labin if he has that pain; and from it labinah meaning clay. Ibn al‑Sikkit says it is his brother biliban of his mother, and one does not say bilaban of his mother, only the milk that is drunk. The thing Ibn al‑Sikkit denied is not denied, because it is taken from the drunk milk, as if they were t‑al‑bana laban, as is said … It should be said: it is from the milk, but it is not said bilaban of his mother, rather it is said biliban of his mother.

From what is similar to this milk: the chest, with an open lam. Al‑luban: the khandur, as if it were milk that sweetens from a tree. The analogy is one. From it al‑lubana, which is the need. It may be applied to the entry by a strike of analogy, except that it is nearer to rarity.
